items.title: Calculating kinetic energy
items.keyIdea: Kinetic energy KE = ½ m v² with mass in kg and speed in m/s, giving joules. Square the speed, keep the half, and rearrange with v = √(2 KE / m). Doubling speed multiplies KE by four because of v².

items.title: Alternating and direct current
items.keyIdea: Direct current (d.c.) from cells and batteries keeps one direction; alternating current (a.c.) from the mains reverses each half-cycle. UK mains is about 230 V at 50 Hz. Read pd–time graphs: flat for d.c., waving through zero for a.c.

items.title: Factorising a difference of two squares
items.keyIdea: Expressions of the form a² − b² factorise as (a + b)(a − b). Both terms must be perfect squares with a minus between them. Handle coefficients such as 9x² − 25 as (3x + 5)(3x − 5). Sums like x² + 49 do not use this pattern over the reals.

items.title: Comparing and ordering numbers
items.keyIdea: Compare two two-digit numbers by place value: look at the tens digit first, then the ones if the tens match. Write the result with >, = or <, and order a set from smallest to largest the same way.

items.title: Fast & Slow Earth Changes
items.keyIdea: Earth's surface changes in two speeds: fast changes like volcanic eruptions and earthquakes happen in seconds or minutes, and slow changes like wind and water wearing rock away (erosion) take years.

items.title: Fluent adding and subtracting within 20
items.keyIdea: Fluent within 20 means you know from memory every sum of two one-digit numbers, and the related take-aways, using doubles and near-doubles as anchors — without recounting every counter each time.

items.title: Simple Chance Experiments
items.keyIdea: A chance experiment repeats a trial, like a coin flip or a dice roll, and records each outcome in a tally. The expected number is trials × chance: 20 flips × ½ = 10 heads. Real results wobble around it, the coin has no memory of a streak, and more trials give a share closer to the expected one.

items.title: Drawing particle diagrams
items.keyIdea: Draw particles as same-sized circles: neat and touching in solids, touching but jumbled in liquids, far apart and fast in gases.

items.title: Friction & Surfaces
items.keyIdea: Friction is a force between two surfaces that rub together. It always acts against the motion. Rough surfaces like carpet and sandpaper make more friction than smooth ones like ice, so a toy car given the same push stops sooner on a rough floor.

items.title: Asking scientific questions
items.keyIdea: Scientists ask how, why and where questions about the world. There are different ways to find out the answers: watch something change over time, do a test, or look it up in a book or ask an expert. A question about what you like best is not one science can answer.

items.title: Contact & Non-Contact Forces
items.keyIdea: Some forces only work when two things touch: a kick, a push on a door, friction. These are contact forces. Other forces act across a gap: a magnet pulls a paper clip before it touches it, and gravity pulls a falling apple. These are non-contact forces, and they get weaker as the gap grows.

items.title: What Plants Need to Grow
items.keyIdea: A plant needs water, light and warmth to grow and stay well. With no water it dries up and flops. In the dark it goes pale and weak. In the cold it hardly grows. Too much water is bad too, because the roots sit in water.

items.title: Rounding to 10, 100, 1000
items.keyIdea: To round a number, find the two multiples it sits between and choose the nearer one. Look at the digit just right of the place you round to: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down. So 4,367 is 4,370 to the nearest 10, 4,400 to the nearest 100 and 4,000 to the nearest 1000.

items.title: Parallel and perpendicular lines
items.keyIdea: A horizontal line lies flat, like the ground, and a vertical line goes straight up and down. Parallel lines go the same way and keep the same gap all along, so they never meet. Perpendicular lines meet or cross at a right angle, a square corner. Length and tilt do not matter: two slanted lines can b

items.title: Rainforest Layers
items.keyIdea: A rainforest has four layers. From the ground up, they are the forest floor, the understory, the canopy and the emergent layer. The floor is dark and damp, with rotting leaves. Small trees and bushes grow in the shady understory. The canopy is a thick roof of treetops, and most animals live there be

items.title: Reading Food Web Diagrams
items.keyIdea: A food web is many food chains joined together. Each arrow points from the food to the eater. Every chain starts with a producer, a plant that makes food from sunlight. items.keyIdea: Gravity is a pulling force between the Earth and every object. It pulls things towards the centre of the Earth all the time. items.title: Material properties vocabulary
items.keyIdea: Use exact words in pairs: transparent/translucent/opaque, conductor/insulator, soluble/insoluble, flexible/rigid, magnetic/non-magnetic.

items.title: Living, Dead & Never Alive
items.keyIdea: Everything belongs to one of three groups. Living things are alive now: they eat or drink, grow and have babies. items.keyIdea: Animals have babies in two main ways. Birds, reptiles, most fish, frogs and insects lay eggs, and the babies hatch out. items.title: Reading tables
items.keyIdea: A table sorts information into rows and columns. In a bus timetable each column is one bus and each row is one stop, so you go down the bus's column to the stop's row and read the time. A dash means the bus does not stop there. items.keyIdea: Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is changed, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. items.title: Linear number sequences
items.keyIdea: A linear sequence uses the same step from each term to the next. That step is the term-to-term rule. It can add, take away, or use a decimal, such as +4, −3 or +0.5. The 10th term is the first term plus 9 of those steps, not 10. If the step changes, as in 2, 4, 8, 16, the sequence is not linear.

items.title: Animal Migration
items.keyIdea: Migration is a long trip an animal makes, and then it comes back. Animals travel to find food, to have babies, or to follow the seasons. items.keyIdea: Levers, pulleys and gears can let a smaller force have a greater effect. On a lever, push farther from the pivot than the load sits. items.keyIdea: Each statistics word names one job. Frequency counts how often a value comes up. The mode is the most common value. The median is the middle value once the data is in order. items.title: Savanna & Grassland Animals
items.keyIdea: A grassland is a wide open habitat of grass with few trees. The African savanna has lions, zebras, wildebeest, elephants, giraffes and cheetahs. items.title: Reading and drawing circuit diagrams
items.keyIdea: A circuit diagram uses standard symbols instead of pictures. A cell is a long thin line and a short thick line. A battery is two or more cells joined. A lamp is a circle with a cross. items.title: Place value: × 10 and ÷ 10
items.keyIdea: Each place is worth ten times the place to its right, so × 10 moves every digit one place left and ÷ 10 moves it one place right.

items.title: Times tables for 2, 5 and 10
items.keyIdea: A times table fact like 5 × 3 = 15 tells you how many are in equal groups. The 10s facts all end in 0. The 5s facts are half of the 10s facts. The 2s facts are doubles. Each times fact gives a division fact too: 5 × 3 = 15, so 15 ÷ 5 = 3 and 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Those facts make a fact family.

items.title: Times tables for 3, 4 and 8
items.keyIdea: The 4s are double the 2s, and the 8s are double the 4s: 2 × 7 = 14, 4 × 7 = 28, 8 × 7 = 56. The 3s are 2 lots and 1 more lot: 3 × 8 = 16 + 8 = 24. Every times fact gives a division fact: 8 × 4 = 32, so 32 ÷ 4 = 8. Every 8s number is a 4s number, but only every other 4s number is an 8s number.

items.title: Desert Animals
items.keyIdea: A desert is a habitat with very little rain or snow, under about 250 mm a year. Deserts can be hot or cold, but they are always dry. items.title: What Ocean Animals Need
items.keyIdea: Ocean animals need the same things as land animals: food, a safe place to hide (shelter), oxygen and the right conditions. A clownfish eats plankton and hides in an anemone. A fish takes oxygen from the water with its gills, but a dolphin swims up to breathe air. The ocean is not the same everywhere

items.keyIdea: The 12 × 12 square has 144 facts, but once you know the 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 tables and that a fact and its turnaround match (7 × 9 = 9 × 7), only 10 new facts are left, all in the 7, 9, 11 and 12 tables. items.title: Polar Animals
items.keyIdea: The Arctic, in the far north, is a frozen ocean with land around it: polar bears, Arctic foxes and walruses live there. items.title: Where Are the Poles?
items.keyIdea: Earth has two poles. On a globe, the North Pole is at the very top and the South Pole is at the very bottom. The Equator is an imaginary line round the middle, halfway between them. items.title: Coasts & Beaches
items.keyIdea: A coast is the place where the land meets the sea; a beach is the part of the coast you can walk on. Coasts are not all the same: some are sandy, some are rocky and some are muddy. Each kind has its own plants and animals, such as lugworms and marram grass on sand, limpets and seaweed on rocks, and

items.title: Fluent adding and subtracting within 100
items.keyIdea: Being fluent within 100 means choosing a quick, reliable way for the numbers in front of you. Split both numbers into tens and ones when no number is near a ten (46 + 37 = 70 + 13 = 83). items.title: Fractions as division
items.keyIdea: a/b means a ÷ b: sharing a wholes equally between b people gives each person a/b.

items.title: Addition and subtraction word problems
items.keyIdea: A word problem is a little story with numbers. Act it out with objects or a quick drawing, then ask: do more come, or do some go away? items.title: Risk, Uncertainty, and Cognitive Bias
items.keyIdea: A risk is a choice where the odds can be known (1 in 6 for a dice); uncertainty is a choice where nobody can know the odds (whether you will like a new club). Our brains judge both with shortcuts that can mislead: the availability bias (vivid stories make rare things feel likely), present bias (now

items.title: Arctic vs Antarctic
items.keyIdea: The Arctic and the Antarctic are both icy and cold, but they are opposites. The Arctic, round the North Pole, is a frozen ocean with land all round it; people live there in towns, and polar bears hunt on the sea ice. The Antarctic, round the South Pole, is a huge continent of land covered in thick i

items.title: Ocean Animal Variety
items.keyIdea: The ocean is home to a huge variety of animals. They come in every size, from a clownfish about as long as your hand to the blue whale, the biggest animal that has ever lived. They come in many shapes: star-shaped sea stars, long thin eels, flat rays, spiky pufferfish and octopuses with eight arms.

items.title: Wide Independent Reading Across Genres
items.keyIdea: Reading widely means reading many kinds of text, not just many books: different genres (mystery, science fiction, historical fiction, fantasy), different forms (novels, short stories, poems, plays, non-fiction such as memoir), and books from different periods and cultures. items.title: Ordering Numbers to 1000
items.keyIdea: To compare two numbers up to 1000, line up the places and scan from the left: hundreds first, then tens, then ones. The first place where the digits differ decides. Record it with >, = or <, and order a set by doing the same scan.

items.keyIdea: To multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number, partition it into tens and ones, multiply each part with a times-table fact and add: 23 × 4 = 80 + 12 = 92. items.title: Momentum
items.keyIdea: Momentum is mass times velocity: p = m × v, measured in kg m/s. Because velocity has a direction, momentum is a vector: choose one direction as positive and anything moving the other way has negative momentum. A heavy, slow object can have more momentum than a light, fast one.

items.title: Observing with simple equipment
items.keyIdea: Scientists look closely. A hand lens makes small things look bigger, so you can see details that were there all along. Move it until the view is sharp, then describe what you see with looking words: colour, shape, size, texture and pattern. Use your observations to compare and identify things, and p

items.title: Comparing and ordering measurements
items.keyIdea: Measure first, then compare the numbers with their units. Start a ruler at 0, read scales carefully, and use the same unit for both things. Record the result with > (greater than), < (less than) or = (the same), and order several measurements from smallest to greatest.

items.title: Coordinates on a grid
items.keyIdea: (x, y) means go x across along the x-axis, then y up, starting from the origin (0, 0).

items.title: Ionic bonding and lattices
items.keyIdea: When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons transfer from the metal atoms to the non-metal atoms, making positive and negative ions. items.title: Area by Tiling
items.keyIdea: Tile a rectangle with unit squares in rows. Every row has the same number of squares, so the area is the number of rows times the number in each row. That is the same as multiplying the two side lengths: a 4 by 6 rectangle has 4 × 6 = 24 square units. Area is measured in squares, such as cm² or m².

items.title: Finding efficient methods
items.keyIdea: Look for what repeats, then use it to count faster or to say what comes next. Things in pairs can be counted in 2s, hands in 5s and packs of ten in 10s, and the total is the same as counting in 1s. Adding 1 always gives the next number. On a hundred square, 10 more is one row down.

items.title: Purpose, audience, and context
items.keyIdea: Before you judge a text, ask three questions. Purpose: what does the writer want the reader to think or do? Audience: who is it written for? items.title: Simple tests and experiments
items.keyIdea: A simple test answers a question by trying it out. Change one thing, keep everything else the same, look closely at what happens and write it down. Then use what you saw to answer the question, even if it is not what you guessed.

items.title: Calculating with measurements
items.keyIdea: Before you add or subtract measurements, put them in the same unit: 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 l = 1000 ml. Then calculate with the numbers and keep the unit on the answer. To find how much longer, heavier or more, find the difference.

items.title: Domain and range
items.keyIdea: The domain of a function is the set of inputs it can take; the range is the set of outputs it actually gives. items.title: Showing Your Working
items.keyIdea: Showing your working means showing how you got an answer, not just the answer. You can use counters, a drawing, a number line or words. Then anyone can check it, and you can check other people's working too.

items.title: Fair testing
items.keyIdea: A fair test changes one variable, measures one variable and keeps every other variable the same. Then any difference in the results must come from the one thing you changed. Repeating a test helps you spot a reading that went wrong.

items.title: Evaluating Arguments in Non-Fiction
items.keyIdea: To evaluate an argument, find the main claim, then test the support. Is the evidence relevant to the claim, and is there enough of it? Is the reasoning sound, or does it lean on tricks like attacking the person? Check who is writing, then decide which side is more convincing and say why.

items.title: Percentage increase and decrease
items.keyIdea: Use a multiplier: increase by r% means × (1 + r/100), decrease means × (1 − r/100); divide by it to find the original.

items.title: Ocean Depth Zones
items.keyIdea: Sunlight fades as it goes down into the sea, so the open ocean has three zones. The sunlight zone is the top 200 m, where there is plenty of light. items.keyIdea: Every division is a times question with a missing number. 32 ÷ 8 = ? asks 8 × ? = 32, and the missing factor is the answer: 8 × 4 = 32, so 32 ÷ 8 = 4. So you can divide with a times-table fact you already know, and check any division by multiplying back.

items.title: Combustion of fuels
items.keyIdea: Hydrocarbon fuels burn by reacting with oxygen. With plenty of oxygen, combustion is complete: the carbon becomes carbon dioxide and the hydrogen becomes water, as in CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. items.title: Tides, Waves & Currents
items.keyIdea: The sea moves in three different ways. Waves are made by wind blowing over the water; a wave carries energy along, but the water itself mostly stays in place. items.title: Human impact on environments
items.keyIdea: People change the places where plants and animals live. items.keyIdea: The ocean floor is not flat. Near the land it is shallow, then it drops down to wide, flat plains far below. items.title: Edges, vertices, and faces
items.keyIdea: We describe a 3-D shape by counting its parts. A face is a flat side. An edge is a straight line where two faces meet. items.keyIdea: The mean is one kind of average. To find it, add up all the values to get the total, then divide by how many values there are: mean = total ÷ number of values. items.title: Charges and masses of subatomic particles
items.keyIdea: Protons (+1, mass 1) and neutrons (0, mass 1) sit in the tiny nucleus; electrons (−1, mass almost 0) are outside it.

items.title: Inherited characteristics
items.keyIdea: Plants and animals get some of their features from their parents. items.keyIdea: One number can be shown in different ways: as a numeral (346), as base-ten blocks (3 hundreds, 4 tens and 6 ones) and as a point on a number line. items.keyIdea: Scientists write down what they find as they go, so they do not forget and can answer their question. Pick the record that fits the question. items.keyIdea: Frequency f is the number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz): 1 Hz is one wave per second. The time period T is the time for one whole wave, in seconds. items.keyIdea: Every sound is made by something vibrating: moving back and forth very fast. items.keyIdea: Money is counted by the value of the coins, not by how many coins there are. 100 pence (100p) make one pound (£1), so £1.45 is 145p. items.title: Acids, alkalis and pH
items.keyIdea: pH runs from 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline; indicators show it with colour.

items.keyIdea: Light travels from a light source and bounces off the surfaces it hits. This bouncing is called reflection. items.keyIdea: An honest conversation goes after the problem, not the person. items.keyIdea: When two designs try to solve the same problem, test them both in the same way and write down what happens. Repeat each test a few times, because one try can go wrong. items.title: Cloud Types
items.keyIdea: Air always holds some water vapour, a gas you cannot see. When damp air rises, it cools, and the vapour condenses into tiny drops of water (or bits of ice, if it is cold enough). items.title: Minibeast Habitats
items.keyIdea: A micro-habitat is a tiny home, like the space under a log, the soil, a leaf or a pond. Each one has its own conditions: damp or dry, dark or light, wet or on land. items.title: Picture & Bar Graphs
items.keyIdea: A picture graph uses one picture for each thing counted. A bar graph uses bars instead. Each bar starts at 0 and stops on the line that matches its number, so you read a bar by the number at its top. Give the graph a title and label both axes: the side axis counts, the bottom axis names the groups.

items.title: Balanced & Unbalanced Forces
items.keyIdea: Forces are pushes and pulls, measured in newtons (N). items.title: Reactions that release or absorb heat
items.keyIdea: Exothermic reactions give energy out (temperature rises); endothermic reactions take energy in (temperature falls).

items.title: Sound Travels Through Materials
items.keyIdea: Sound is made by vibrations, and those vibrations travel through a material, called a medium, to your ear. items.keyIdea: Wind is moving air, and the Sun sets it moving. The Sun heats the Earth's surface unevenly: dry land such as sand or rock warms faster than water. items.keyIdea: A switch opens and closes a gap in a circuit. When the switch is closed, its metal parts touch, the circuit is complete and current flows, so a lamp lights or a buzzer sounds. items.title: The Sun is a star
items.keyIdea: The Sun is a star: a huge ball of hot, glowing gas that makes its own light and heat. It is the closest star to Earth. items.title: Light Travels in Straight Lines
items.keyIdea: Light travels in straight lines from a light source. items.keyIdea: To order three things by length, line up their starting ends and compare the other ends. items.title: Why seasons change
items.keyIdea: Through the year, the number of hours of daylight changes. items.keyIdea: Penguins are birds that cannot fly. Their wings are stiff flippers, so they are excellent swimmers. The emperor penguin is the biggest, about as tall as a 6-year-old child. items.title: Reading distance–time graphs
items.keyIdea: On a distance–time graph, flat means stopped, steeper means faster, and the gradient is the speed.

items.title: Finding halves and quarters

items.title: Objects and materials
items.keyIdea: An object is a thing; a material is what the thing is made of.

items.title: Naming everyday materials
items.keyIdea: Everyday things are made of materials such as wood, plastic, glass, metal, rock and fabric.

items.title: Describing material properties
items.keyIdea: We describe materials with pairs of words: hard or soft, stiff or bendy, shiny or dull, waterproof or not.

items.title: Choosing the right material
items.keyIdea: We choose a material because its properties suit the job.

items.title: Grouping materials
items.keyIdea: We can group materials by a property, such as hard or soft, or shiny or dull.

items.keyIdea: A solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, and a gas spreads out to fill any space.

items.title: Solids, liquids and gases
items.keyIdea: We group materials as solids, liquids or gases by how they behave: keep shape, flow, or spread out.

items.title: Heating and cooling changes
items.keyIdea: Heating can melt a solid and boil a liquid; cooling can freeze a liquid; we measure the temperature in °C.

items.title: Dissolving and solutions
